title: Pull your ears
hookLine: nodding Moggallana is given remedies for drowsiness: from pulling your ears to walking

cards: The breath is slow, the room is warm, and then your chin dips toward your chest, and you jerk back up, hoping no one saw. Anyone who has sat to meditate knows that moment.

In the Book of Sevens, it happens to Moggallana, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, well-known in the tradition for his powers of mind. He's sitting in meditation near a village in Magadha, and he keeps nodding.
The Buddha, the text says, sees it from far away, and comes to him with a list of remedies.

teach.b: Are you nodding, Moggallana? Yes, sir. Then comes a ladder, each step tried only if the one before doesn't work.
First: whatever thought you were on when drowsiness came, stop giving it attention. Second: think over a teaching you've learned. Third: recite a teaching out loud, in detail.
Fourth: pull both your earlobes and rub your limbs with your hands.
Fifth: get up, wash your eyes with water, and look around in every direction, and up at the stars. Sixth: bring to mind the perception of light, the idea of daytime, day and night alike.

Seventh: walk up and down, with your senses gathered in. And if none of that works? Eighth: lie down on your right side, like a lion, mindful, with the thought of getting up again, and when you wake, get up promptly.
No one is scolded. Sleepiness isn't treated as a sin, just a state with causes and cures.
Thinking, then talking, then the body, then cold water and open sky, then movement, and last of all, permission to rest. The order matters.
The sutta goes on with advice on pride and on argument, but the ear-pulling is the part people remember.

how: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions still give these remedies for sleepiness, such as opening the eyes, standing, or switching to walking meditation, and some retreats offer standing or walking periods for exactly this.

o: the trance of very deep meditation
a restless urge to get up and pace

games.q: pull your ears: tap the pairs.
p: the chief disciple who nodded off
wash your eyes, look at the stars
lie down like a lion, mindful

s: only beginners get sleepy in meditation, according to the texts
the sutta's nodding monk is Moggallana, a chief disciple.
the Buddha's last remedy is permission to lie down and rest
on the right side, like a lion, intending to get up again.
the remedies are meant to be tried in order
each step is offered if the one before doesn't work.

games.q: you're meditating and keep nodding off. you've tried thinking of a teaching and reciting one. what's the next remedy in the sutta?
o: pull your earlobes and rub your limbs.
games.why: pull both earlobes and rub your limbs. after that come cold water and the stars, then walking, and last of all, rest.

practice: Check your alertness right now, honestly. If it's low, try the fourth step: take both earlobes between thumb and finger and give them a slow pull, then rub your hands together and along your arms.
If you're already alert, rest with the breath and learn what alertness feels like, so you'll know it when it fades.

wordCard.voice: pacala. The Pali word for nodding or drowsiness, the state of Moggallana in the Book of Sevens, met by the Buddha with a ladder of remedies from changing the thought to looking at the stars. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pacala: nodding, drowsiness; the sutta's name, 'the nodding discourse.'

carryVoice: Your line: climb the ladder. Rest is a rung too; it's just the last one. See you tomorrow.
